title: The proposed EU Quantum Act: from quantum readiness to industrial capacity
content:
The European Commission’s proposal for a Quantum Act brings Europe’s quantum ambitions into sharper focus. For businesses, it combines opportunities to commercialise quantum technologies with a renewed imperative to prepare for their security implications.

In our earlier article on Quantum Transition, we explained why organisations should begin preparing for the quantum transition before the regulatory framework catches up. The Commission’s proposal of 25 November 2026 marks a new step: a proposed Quantum Act aims to strengthen the European Union’s competitiveness and resilience in the global quantum ecosystem. Its more specific objectives are to translate research strengths into products and services, strengthen supply chains and support the transition to post-quantum cryptography. It also lays the groundwork for a Sovereign Tech Equity Fund (STEF). The message for businesses remains unchanged: legislative developments should inform, not postpone, preparedness. 1

title: Is ageing good business? The growing market for longevity
content:
Growing interest in living longer, healthier lives is driving the expansion of the global longevity market. At Dittmar & Indrenius’ Is Ageing Good Business? event, experts discussed the science, consumer demand, investment landscape and commercial opportunities shaping the healthtech sector.

Ahead of Slush, one of the world’s leading startup events, Dittmar & Indrenius hosted the side event Is Ageing Good Business? The event attracted a full house keen to explore the scientific and commercial potential of this rapidly growing sector. Following opening remarks by Dittmar & Indrenius Partners Anna Haapanen and Juli Mansnérus, Isak Rautio, Founder and Host of Futucast, moderated a panel discussion.

According to Rautio, longevity, the art and science of living as long and as healthily as possible, has attracted increasing attention in recent years. While extending healthy lifespans has always been a concern in medicine, consumers are now taking a growing interest in the subject. This is partly due to podcasts exploring longevity and public figures such as biohacker Bryan Johnson, whose motto is “Don’t die”.

title: IPI restrictions in medical device procurement: from early experience to the first review
content:
Over a year into the EU’s IPI restrictions on medical device procurement, early cases highlight challenges with the EUR 5 million threshold and the 50% cap on Chinese-origin supplies. The first review of the IPI Regulation brings these issues into focus for contracting authorities and suppliers.

The International Procurement Instrument (IPI) Regulation (EU) 2022/1031 allows restrictions on access to EU procurement markets to encourage third countries to open theirs to EU companies. This sits within a broader shift towards using procurement to advance EU strategic interests, also reflected in the ‘Buy European’ preferences envisaged in the Commission’s September 2026 proposal for a Public Procurement Act.

title: The concept of scientific research in data protection law: current state and future prospects?
content: The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (“GDPR”) applies also where personal data is processed for scientific research purposes. However, the GDPR does not formally define “scientific research”, and so far, there has not been a clear consensus on the definition of the term under the GDPR.1 The distinction matters, as processing personal data for scientific research purposes benefits from specific rules and flexibilities under the GDPR, including, for example, presumed compatibility of further processing and the possibility of longer retention under Article 5, subject to Article 89 safeguards. Article 17 also provides a conditional exception to erasure where erasure would make research impossible or seriously impair its objectives.

title: Navigating the tricky borders of AI scribes in healthcare
content:
The potential of AI has definitely not been lost on the healthcare sector. AI has the ability to solve many long-standing problems in modern healthcare: lack of resources, risks of human error and difficulties in serving a rapidly evolving patient base. While risks and concerns exist, the AI transformation of the patient journey and other healthcare processes seems inevitable, both in the private and public sectors.

AI scribes, namely AI tools with the ability to convert human interactions into transcripts, visit summaries and other clinical documentation, appear to be a key example of this development. The typical use case is that an appointment between a patient and medical professional is recorded by an AI tool, converted into text and arranged into legally required medical record entries. As a result, the doctor can focus fully on the patient interaction without having to take meticulous notes and save time afterwards as the AI tool has already drafted the required entries.

Legally, things get interesting when we look at what the AI scribe actually does and the extent to which the medical record entries and subsequent clinical activities rely on the AI scribe’s output.

title: Disputes for Breakfast: Sovittelun myytit 25.11.2026
content:
Sovittelusta puhutaan paljon, mutta mitä siitä todella tiedetään? Tässä webinaarissa sovittelijat Ralf Lindbäck, Heidi Merikalla-Teir ja Petri Taivalkoski käyvät Helen Lehdon ja Laura Gordinin kanssa läpi yleisimpiä sovitteluun liittyviä myyttejä ja pohtivat yhdessä, pitävätkö ne paikkansa vai onko aika kumota ne.

Keskusteluun nousevat muun muassa seuraavat väittämät:

  • “Kaikki sovittelumenettelyt ovat samanlaisia”
  • “Sovittelussa ei ole järkeä, kun osapuolten neuvottelut ovat olleet tuloksettomat”
  • “Sovittelussa ei tarvita avustajaa”
  • “Sovitteluun ei tarvitse valmistautua”
  • “Sovitteluun voi osallistua kuka tahansa yrityksen edustajana – sillä ei juuri ole väliä”
  • “Sovitteluun ei kannata mennä, koska vastapuoli saa tietää keissimme heikkoudet”

content:

title: Palkka-avoimuusdirektiivi – kaikkia työnantajia koskevat velvoitteet 9.12.2026
content:
EU:n palkka-avoimuusdirektiivi (2023/970) pannaan Suomessa täytäntöön muun muassa tasa-arvolain muutoksilla, joiden on ehdotettu tulevan voimaan 1.1.2027. Uudistus koskee kaikkia työnantajia, myös pieniä ja keskisuuria yrityksiä, ja tuo mukanaan konkreettisia velvoitteita, joihin on syytä tutustua hyvissä ajoin.

Palkka-avoimuutta koskevan webinaarisarjamme ensimmäisessä osassa asianajaja Nana Karanen käy läpi direktiivin perusteita sekä ne velvoitteet, jotka koskevat kaikkia työnantajia organisaation koosta riippumatta.

Webinaarissa käsitellään ainakin:

  • Palkkatiedot työnhakijalle: mitä tietoa on kerrottava, missä muodossa ja milloin
  • Palkkahistorian kysymiskielto: mitä rekrytointiprosessista on poistettava
  • Palkan ja palkkatasojen määrittämiskriteerit: mitä on asetettava henkilöstön saataville helposti ja ilman erillistä pyyntöä
  • Tiedonsaantioikeus: mitä työntekijä voi pyytää, mitä työnantajan on annettava ja miten tietosuoja rajoittaa tiedon antamista
  • Käytännön toimenpidelista: konkreettiset askeleet, jotka jokaisen työnantajan on otettava ennen lain voimaantuloa

title: Data centre register proposal: what data centre providers in Finland should prepare for?
content:
The Finnish Government’s proposal (HE 282/2026 vp) on 29 October 2026 introduces mandatory notifications for data centres to the National Emergency Supply Agency (NESA, Fin. Huoltovarmuuskeskus). The aim is to contribute to a more comprehensive and anticipatory situational picture of the data centre investments, intended use and ownership of data centres, electricity demand and infrastructure needs in Finland. The proposed entry into force is 1 April 2027.

Broad scope and early notification. The register would cover planned, under-construction and operational data centres in Finland with planned or actual installed IT power demand of at least 0.5 MW. This refers to IT equipment threshold, not total grid connection capacity. Notifications would be due within 30 days of signing a grid connection agreement and, in all cases, before construction starts. Data centres within the scope of the act that have already concluded an electricity network agreement, are under construction, or are in operation would be required to submit a notification by 30 June 2027.
